newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end mixed; blue chips fall on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end mixed; blue chips fall on profit-taking.

text.p: Stocks closed mixed Friday as investors took profits in the high-flying blue chips and shifted to small companies, boosting the lagging Nasdaq market.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended off 10.77 points at 6,813.09 after racking up two straight days of gains. For the week, the index was up 116.61 points.
The Nasdaq composite index rose 8.83 points to 1,379.85, ending up 16.01 points for the week.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,380 to 1,098 on heavy volume of 574 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"With a couple of good days behind us, it looks some players are taking profits ahead of the weekend," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "But it's modest and the market is giving back very little ground."
A strong rally in bonds on new evidence that the economy is fighting off inflation boosted the blue chips earlier in the day, but they fell victim to late profit-taking.

The good news on inflation came from a Commerce Department report showing the nation's Gross Domestic Product grew by an annual rate of 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter, more than double the third quarter rate of 2.1 percent and well ahead of forecasts for 3.9 percent growth.
Despite the strength, the GDP price index rose only 1.8 percent, showing little if any inflation threat.

In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond gained a full point, which lowered its yield to 6.79 percent from Thursday's close of 6.87 percent. The yield and the price move in opposite directions.
"Investors have been watching the yield on the long bond very carefully because many see 7 percent as a level where stocks may give back ground," said Ackerman.
"We did see a little profit-taking at the end, but with yields a bit lower there's a sense it's best to stay the course," he said.
Looking past the Dow's marginal decline, the signs from the market were mostly positive.
Also important, according to market tradition, was that the Dow finished January some 360 points higher than it started the month.
"As goes January, so goes the year," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage, reciting a Wall Street adage.

The so-called "January Barometer" -- which by the purest method actually tracks the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index -- calls for the market to finish the year higher when it rises in January and lower when it falls in the month.
According to data from the Hirsch Organisation, the barometer has forecast the market's direction in 41 out of the last 46 years.
The S&P 500 closed at 786.16, up 1.99 for the day and up 45.42 points or 6 percent for the month.
Drug stocks remained strong. Warner-Lambert Co. rose three to 81, Pfizer Inc. gained 1-3/4 to 92-1/2 and Schering-Plough Corp. climbed 1-5/8 to 72-1/8.
"The drug stocks continue to power up," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "They offer a classic defensive posture along with growth opportunity."

In individual issues, Mercury Finance Corp. was the NYSE's most active stock, plummeting 12-7/8 to two on more than 35 million shares in volume after the company said earlier this week that it found problems in its bookkeeping that caused it to overstate earnings by $90 million over four years.
On Friday, Mercury said would be unable to pay $17 million in commercial debt due the same day.

Radisys Corp. skidded 11-1/2 to 46 after the company said the Securities and Exchange Commission was examining its inventory accounting. Radisys said it had yet to hear from the SEC since complying with the agency's request for documents.
The American Stock Exchange index rose 0.11 to 588.77.
The Russell 2000 index up 1.16 points to 369.45. The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 0.78 to 411.98. The average share was up 8 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,575.793 up 19.007 or 0.25 percent.
